3.text: will be observed, are the same in regard to the owner of game (Pičvuˊčin).¹

4.text: A shaman who visits the land of mice finds that their ways of life are

5.text: quite human. He is requested to help a woman who is suffering from a

6.text: severe cold and sharp pain in her throat. When looking at her, he notices

7.text: on her neck a thin noose of grass, such as Chukchee children make to catch

8.text: mice. He destroys the noose, and the Mouse-Woman recovers. In return

9.text: for his services, the Mouse-People give him the choicest fawn-skins. On his

10.text: return to our world, however, these prove to be dry leaves and pieces of bark.

11.text: In most cases, animals, while personating human beings, retain some of

12.text: their former qualities, which identify them as beings of a special class acting

13.text: in a human way, but different from mankind. For instance, a whale, when

14.text: carrying away a young woman, continues to be a whale, and even makes her

15.text: pick out the barnacles from his skin; polar bears have diving-matches, and

16.text: catch seals with their paws; Fox-Woman keeps her strong smell, and Goose-

17.text: Woman, her aversion to animal food, which may soil her clean white dress.

18.text: Amulets of animal origin — for instance, a dried skin, a head or a skull,

19.text: a claw or a feather — are also considered susceptible of like sudden trans-

20.text: formation, in which they acquire the qualities of living animals of a corre-

21.text: sponding species, and perform certain tasks. Afterward they return to their

22.text: former shape. In one tale, a dried skin of an ermine transforms itself into a

23.text: living ermine, which, in turn, transforms itself into a large polar bear. In

24.text: this shape the amulet is sent by its “owner” across the sea to harm an enemy.

25.text: When unable to do this, it comes back, and is blamed by its “owner.”²

26.text: The next stage (the fourth), as said before, supposes a complete distinction

27.text: between the two forms of the object; and the idea of the transfigured form

28.text: is replaced by the conception of a certain anthropomorphous “genius,” who

29.text: co-exists with the object, and lives within its material shape, but may at will

30.text: leave it, and appear separately. In studying this stage we must, however,

31.text: distinguish between the smaller material objects (such as stones, trees, etc.) and

32.text: the larger unities, as forests, lakes, rivers, mountains, and other localities.

33.text: In the development of the religious ideas of the Chukchee, the conception

34.text: of smaller material objects belonged to the more primitive stages (first or

35.text: second), and separable “genii” were not attached to them: at least, the develop-

36.text: ment in this direction is not very clear. Thus, as mentioned before, smaller

37.text: material objects are sometimes called g̣êtɪˊnvɪlên (“having a master”); but, as

38.text: will be shown, the Chukchee conception of a “master” coincides with the

39.text: Eskimo “its man” (inua), and represents the “genius.” In reference to smaller

40.text: objects, this idea remained undeveloped, and the objects were more frequently
